body:
Hmm... This feels like one of the effects of `None` not being a real value in mypy. E.g. just this gives an error:

```
d = {'': None} # E: Need type annotation for variable
```

it may also have to do with covariance because the following also errors:

```
e = {}  # type: Dict[str, Union[int, str]]
e.update({str(i): i for i in range(4)})  # error: Argument 1 to "update" of "dict" has incompatible type Dict[str, int]; expected "Union[Mapping[...], Iterable[...]]"
```
I suspect that this is related to type inference + union types. https://github.com/python/mypy/pull/1408 might fix this as well.

This is related to but distinct from #1408. Here we need to infer the key and value types of the dictionary comprehension `{str(i): None for i in range(4)}` that will make its type a subtype of the expected argument type `Union[Mapping[str, Optional[int]], Iterable[Tuple[str, Optional[int]]]]`. (This is `t <: Union[...]`, rather than `Union[...] :> t`; the organization of constraint generation is such that these are different problems, though I'm not sure that they need to be.)

This particular case is complicated by the fact that a `Dict[K, V]` is both a `Mapping[K, V]` and an `Iterable[K]`, which makes the declaration

```
def update(self, m: Union[Mapping[_KT, _VT], Iterable[Tuple[_KT, _VT]]]) -> None: ...
```

a bit of a lie. Suppose you have a `d: Dict[K, V]` and `m: Dict[Tuple[K, V], W]` and you call `d.update(m)`. Then mypy will allow the call, but python will really add the key-value pairs of `m` to those of `d`, creating a dictionary with some keys of type `K` and some keys of type `Tuple[K, V]`. I assume that `update` internally does something like an `isinstance(..., dict)` check, and if the argument is not a `dict`, falls back to the iterator protocol. And so in reality if you pass a `Dict[K, V]` to `update`, then `update` will always have the type corresponding to the `Mapping[_KT, _VT]` option, and never the `Iterable[Tuple[_KT, _VT]]]` option, even if `K` happens to be of the form `Tuple[_KT, _VT]`.

This also means that (even if mypy could infer constraints from `t <: Union[...]`) in the actual call

```
d.update({str(i): None for i in range(4)})
```

we can't infer the key type of the dictionary comprehension from the context alone; it could be either `str` or `Tuple[str, Optional[int]]`. In the latter case, the value type could be anything. So in order to handle this case, we'd have to first work out the key type from the body of the comprehension `str(i): None`, then eliminate the possibility of the comprehension having type `Iterable[Tuple[str, int]]`, then conclude it has type `Mapping[str, Optional[int]]` and use that to infer the value type `Optional[int]` and type check the body of the comprehension. This is probably workable, but unappealing since it's only needed because the stub type for `update` is not entirely accurate.

In practice I found it seems to work well to change the stub for `update` to an overloaded function, like

```
    @overload
    def update(self, m: Mapping[_KT, _VT]) -> None: ...
    @overload
    def update(self, m: Iterable[Tuple[_KT, _VT]]) -> None: ...
```

Now if the argument is a `Dict[K, V]` for yet-unknown types `K` and `V`, the first overload will be selected, even though both could match, simply because it is the first one. Then the rest of inference goes through successfully.

Can you start with making update() an overloaded function? That seems a
no-brainer regardless of the rest of the issue. (I think it may have
started out as overloaded, and when we added Union support we may have been
a little too enthusiastic about replacing all overloads with unions.)

issue.title: Mypy error on assigning an empty dict to Union variable
issue.body:
This fails:

``` py
d = {} # type: Union[Dict[str, int], List[int]]
```

with error message:

```
error: Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type Dict[None, None],
variable has type "Union[Dict[str, int], List[int]]")
```

This also fails with a similar error message:

``` py
d = [] # type: Union[Dict[str, int], List[int]]
```

```
error: Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type List[None],
variable has type "Union[Dict[str, int], List[int]]")
```

This works however:

``` py
d = {"abc":123} # type: Union[Dict[str, int], List[int]]
```

I was expecting empty dict to work with `Union`, since the following 2 statements work:
- `d = {} # type: Dict[str, int]`
- `d = 3 # type: Union[int, str]`

body: Yes, making `update` an overloaded function will fix this case, and I don't propose to do anything further here at the moment.
Thanks -- shall we close this issue? Or do we need to keep it open as a reminder of the remaining problem?
Yes, this can be closed now.
